headline: High risk of prompt injection and cascading errors from ECC into Plane; shared write-capable workspace also creates data-leak and conflict exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC ingests files, MCP configs, hooks, and session summaries, and Plane exposes file uploads and hyperlinks. That creates a plausible content bridge where attacker-controlled Plane artifacts could be treated as instructions by ECC. The interaction is inferred from documented surfaces, not directly observed, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF Plane content is copied into ECC-managed files or MCP inputs, instruction-like text can be parsed as commands.
IF ECC hooks or skills process uploaded Plane artifacts without provenance checks, prompt injection becomes reachable.
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of Plane exports into ECC-managed files.
Review and sanitize any Plane text before placing it in MCP or hook inputs.
Use separate workspaces for ECC and Plane artifacts.
Turn off unused ECC hooks for the session.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for imported content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC reads and writes local files and handles session summaries, skills, and security findings; Plane accepts file uploads and broad network egress. If both touch the same workspace, sensitive content can flow from ECC-managed files into Plane uploads or API calls. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default use, but not directly evidenced, so medium fits.
conditions: IF ECC and Plane share a filesystem or synced folder, files can be copied into Plane uploads.
IF ECC session summaries or security findings are stored in the shared workspace, Plane can receive them through file upload or API use.
mitigations: Keep ECC and Plane in separate directories.
Do not upload ECC-generated files into Plane unless redacted.
Restrict Plane uploads to non-sensitive artifacts.
Rotate or isolate any shared credentials immediately.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level access controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; Plane does not write files locally but does have broad network egress and file-upload surfaces. The main conflict is on shared mutable resources: ECC can alter repo state while Plane can concurrently consume or publish related artifacts, and ECC explicitly supports multiple instances with separate roots to avoid overwriting session files. Defaults are dangerous enough to merit high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or workspace, ECC can overwrite files or git state while Plane reads or uploads related artifacts.
IF multiple ECC instances share the default root, session files can collide.
mitigations: Set a separate ECC root immediately.
Keep Plane out of the repo working tree.
Pause one agent before the other edits shared artifacts.
Use git branches for all ECC changes.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC produces code, documentation, and security findings, while Plane handles issues, tasks, and roadmaps. If Plane treats ECC output as authoritative, incorrect findings can cascade into task creation or scheduling decisions. The pathway exists in default workflows, but Plane is not documented as fully autonomous, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF Plane imports ECC-generated findings without verification, incorrect conclusions can become tasks or roadmap items.
IF ECC outputs are copied into Plane issue text, downstream prioritization may rely on unverified claims.
mitigations: Require human review before creating Plane tasks from ECC output.
Mark ECC output as unverified in Plane descriptions.
Cross-check critical findings against source files.
Limit ECC output to summaries, not action directives.
requires-engineering: add validation gates before task creation.

E_compliance.rationale: ECC touches security findings, session summaries, and git history; Plane touches issues, tasks, files, and notes. No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for either agent, so only a limited compliance overlap is visible. Because the profiles are sparse, uncertainty prevents a none verdict, but the blast radius appears small.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in both agents without a shared retention policy, compliance gaps can arise.
IF ECC security findings include sensitive content and Plane retains uploaded files longer than intended, retention mismatch becomes relevant.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in either agent.
Delete stale uploads and session artifacts today.
Document a shared retention rule for both tools.
Review access to ECC secrets immediately.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls.
